nameStory: The 'awned' in this moss's name refers to the bristle-like extensions (awns) on its leaf tips, similar to the awns you might see on wheat or barley grains. Dichelyma comes from Greek words meaning 'double covering,' referring to the protective structures around its reproductive parts that help it survive its aquatic lifestyle.
description: Awned Dichelyma Moss is a rare aquatic moss that forms loose, feathery underwater colonies in clean streams and ponds. The individual plants grow 2-4 inches long with delicate, narrow leaves that give the moss a soft, hair-like appearance when submerged. When water levels drop, you might find it clinging to rocks or logs at the waterline, looking somewhat shriveled and darker green to brownish. This is one of New England's most uncommon mosses, making any sighting quite special.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found in or very close to clean, flowing water - attached to rocks, logs, or tree roots in streams, or sometimes at pond edges where water levels fluctuate

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms loose, feathery clumps that flow gracefully with water currents when submerged, looking almost like underwater hair or fine seaweed

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Extremely narrow and pointed with tiny bristle-like tips (awns) that require a hand lens to see clearly - leaves feel slippery and delicate when wet

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright to medium green when fully hydrated underwater, turning darker olive-green to brownish when exposed to air during dry periods

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels surprisingly soft and silky when wet, almost slippery between your fingers, but becomes somewhat brittle and papery when dried out

habitat: Look for this rare moss in clean, unpolluted streams and spring-fed ponds throughout New England's forested areas. It typically grows attached to submerged rocks, fallen logs, or tree roots where there's gentle to moderate water flow. The moss prefers cooler water temperatures and is most often found in shaded woodland streams rather than open, sunny waterways.

seasonality.spring: Most visible as water levels are high and the moss is fully hydrated, showing its brightest green color and most graceful underwater movement. This is prime time for spotting healthy colonies.
seasonality.summer: May be harder to spot if water levels drop, but look for it clinging to rocks at the waterline where it appears darker and more compressed. Still identifiable by its feathery structure.
seasonality.fall: Often more exposed as water levels typically drop, making it easier to examine closely but appearing less vibrant. The characteristic bristled leaf tips are still visible with a hand lens.
seasonality.winter: Remains green under ice or in flowing water that doesn't freeze completely. In areas where water freezes solid, the moss enters dormancy but survives to regrow in spring.

funFact: This moss is so rare in New England that it's been documented fewer times than some endangered wildflowers - your smartphone probably has more computing power than the total number of confirmed sightings in our region!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other aquatic mosses like Fontinalis (common water moss), but Awned Dichelyma has much more delicate, hair-like leaves with those diagnostic bristle tips. Remember: if it looks like underwater hair with tiny needles on each strand, you've probably found something special.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'moss,' this species lives more like an aquatic plant, which can confuse beginners who expect mosses to grow on land. Its extreme rarity means that any suspected sighting should be photographed and reported to local botanists or natural history organizations.
compareHints: Since this is the only Dichelyma species regularly found in New England, compare it to its relatives in the Fontinalaceae family, particularly Fontinalis species. Awned Dichelyma has much more delicate, narrower leaves and a more feathery overall appearance compared to the broader-leaved, more robust Fontinalis mosses. The bristle-tipped leaves are unique among our regional aquatic mosses.
